claims.text: A high concentration of different principal elements in single-phase high-entropy alloys produces significant lattice distortion.
Lattice distortion creates strong local obstacles to dislocation glide.
Under high-strain-rate loading, these obstacles cause pronounced dislocation pile-up.
Dislocation pile-up culminates in collective dislocation release.
The pile-up and collective-release mechanism enhances both strength and ductility relative to alloys with lower lattice distortion.
Compositional complexity induces severe lattice distortion that impedes individual dislocation glide.
At high strain rates, dislocations accumulate until a critical stress is reached.
Reaching the critical stress causes collective depinning or avalanche-like dislocation motion.
Resistance to initial dislocation motion produces high strength.
Delayed collective plastic flow maintains ductility.
Reducing lattice distortion will lower dynamic strain-rate sensitivity relative to the equiatomic baseline.
Reducing lattice distortion will decrease peak strength relative to the equiatomic baseline.
Reducing lattice distortion will increase uniform plastic flow and ductility relative to the equiatomic baseline at high strain rates.
The higher-distortion baseline will exhibit higher yield and flow stresses.
The higher-distortion baseline will exhibit delayed but abrupt plastic flow in its stress-strain curve.
The equiatomic single-phase FCC baseline is known to have high strength and ductility under dynamic loading.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply to single-phase, near-equiatomic FCC high-entropy alloys at ambient temperature under inert atmosphere.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to multiphase alloys or alloys containing significant precipitates or second-phase particles.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says greater lattice distortion enhances ductility relative to lower-distortion alloys, whereas the predicted outcome says reducing lattice distortion increases uniform plastic flow and ductility relative to the higher-distortion baseline.
